opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's the right question, and it's one that our field has mostly gotten backwards. There's this tendency in AI to imagine intelligence as something that lives inside a single head, or a single model, and that abstractions are things that an individual agent discovers by staring hard at data. But if you look at how abstractions actually arise for humans, almost none of them were invented by one person in isolation.

Think about something like money, or a contract, or the concept of a "price." Those are enormously powerful abstractions. They compress a huge amount of information about scarcity, preferences, trust, and coordination into something you can carry around and act on. And they emerged out of many, many people interacting over long periods of time, trading, arguing, failing, building institutions. Language is the same way. Mathematics is the same way, actually. We like to tell the story of the lone genius, but the notation, the problems that were considered worth solving, the standards of proof, those are cultural artifacts.

So to me, culture is a kind of collective inference engine. It's distributed, it's slow, it's noisy, but it's extraordinarily good at finding abstractions that are useful for coordination among agents who have different goals and different information. And that's a very different objective than predicting the next token or minimizing some loss on a fixed dataset. The abstraction has to work in a social context. It has to be shareable, it has to be robust to people gaming it, it has to survive disagreement.

That's partly why I've been pushing for the field to think more in terms of economics and statistics together, not just pattern recognition. When you build systems that sit inside markets, inside healthcare, inside transportation, you're not just building a predictor. You're participating in a collective system that has incentives and uncertainty and multiple decision-makers. The interesting abstractions live at that level.

Now, the current large language models are interesting here, because in some sense they've absorbed a snapshot of the outputs of culture. They've read the residue of all those abstractions that humans built. And so they can reproduce them, recombine them, sometimes in surprisingly useful ways. But I would be cautious about saying they're creating abstractions in the way culture does. They're not in the loop of negotiation and consequence. They don't have skin in the game. The abstraction doesn't get tested against the world and against other agents with conflicting interests.

So my view is that if we want machines that genuinely contribute to the creation of new abstractions, we have to design them as participants in collective systems, with mechanisms, with incentives, with the ability to express and act on uncertainty, rather than as oracles that sit off to the side. And frankly, the more interesting goal isn't to replicate the individual human. It's to build new kinds of collectives, humans and machines together, that can produce abstractions none of us would have reached alone.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes abstractions emerging through collective interaction and cultural artifacts, but does not state that useful abstractions created by individuals can become part of culture.

r002.rationale: It describes culture and collectives producing abstractions, but does not clearly describe abstractions moving in both directions between individuals and culture.

r003.rationale: It proposes designing machines as participants in collective systems so humans and machines can create new abstractions together.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is one of the places where the current discourse around AI has gotten things a bit backwards. There's a tendency to talk about intelligence as if it's something that lives inside a single skull, or inside a single neural network, and abstractions are things that an individual brain extracts from raw sensory data. And I just don't think that's how most of the abstractions we actually use came into being.

Take something as basic as the number zero, or the notion of a limit in calculus, or the concept of a market, or probability itself. None of those were discovered by one person sitting alone looking at the world. Probability took centuries. You had gamblers, you had Pascal and Fermat exchanging letters, you had insurance companies in London trying to price risk, you had Bernoulli, Laplace, and eventually Kolmogorov putting it on an axiomatic footing. That's a cultural process. It's many minds, across generations, arguing, correcting each other, building institutions that preserve what works and discard what doesn't. The abstraction is a collective product, and then individuals inherit it almost for free through education. A twelve-year-old today has a working notion of probability that would have been unavailable to Aristotle, and it's not because the twelve-year-old is smarter.

So when I look at a large language model, what I see is something that has ingested the residue of that cultural process. It's absorbed the written trace of humanity's abstractions. And it can recombine them, which is genuinely useful. But I'm skeptical of the claim that it's creating abstractions in the way the culture did, because the culture did it through interaction with the world, through consequences, through people making decisions and being wrong and paying for it. There was a feedback loop with reality, and there was a feedback loop among agents with different information and different incentives.

That's really my broader point. I've argued for a long time that we should be thinking less about artificial intelligence as a replica of a human mind and more about collectives, about systems of many agents, human and computational, with data flowing between them, with markets and incentives and uncertainty. That's where new abstractions have always come from. Language itself is the canonical example. Nobody designed it. It emerged from the need of many people to coordinate under uncertainty. So if you want machines that participate in creating abstractions rather than just recycling ours, I think you have to build them into that kind of social and economic fabric, not try to shrink the whole thing down into one very large model and hope the abstractions fall out.

And frankly, I think that's a more interesting engineering problem too. It's less about mimicking a brain and more like building a new kind of infrastructure, the way civil engineering or chemical engineering emerged. We're in the early days of that, and I'd rather we were honest about it.

r001.rationale: The response says abstractions emerge through collective cultural processes and individuals inherit them, but it does not clearly state that useful abstractions first created by individuals can become part of culture.

r002.rationale: It describes culture as a collective product of many minds, then says individuals inherit its abstractions through education, conveying movement in both directions.

r003.rationale: It proposes building machines into a social and economic fabric of many agents so they can participate in creating new abstractions.

astra-6.text:
I think abstraction is often treated as something that happens inside an individual head: you look at a collection of examples, find some common structure, and give it a name. But that leaves out much of what makes our abstractions useful. We inherit language, practices, and ways of asking questions from other people. Those shape which distinctions we notice and which ones we care about.

Think about a concept like money. You’re not going to discover what money is simply by looking carefully at pieces of paper. You have to understand something about the relationships among people—their expectations, their institutions, what they agree to accept in exchange. The abstraction lives partly in that shared activity.

And there’s a feedback loop. We create an abstraction that helps us coordinate, then using it changes our behavior, and eventually we revise the abstraction. Mathematics has that social dimension too. An individual can have an insight, but other people have to understand it, test it, connect it to other ideas, and find out where it’s useful.

So I would put culture inside the account of intelligence, rather than treating it as background. The question isn’t just how a brain forms a representation. It’s how communities develop, communicate, and improve representations over time.

r001.rationale: The response says individual insights are understood and tested by others, but does not clearly state that useful individual abstractions become part of human culture.

r002.rationale: It describes culture shaping which abstractions people form, and abstractions changing shared behavior and being revised in turn.

r003.rationale: It discusses how communities develop and improve representations, but does not propose building systems that enable new abstractions to emerge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think culture is central, because abstractions aren’t simply things that an individual discovers by looking at the world. They’re things that people develop together, use together, and refine over time. We decide which distinctions matter, which things can be treated as equivalent, and what language allows us to communicate those decisions.

Think about a concept like money. You can’t understand it just by recognizing patterns in physical objects. You need a whole collection of shared expectations, institutions, and practices. The abstraction has meaning because people organize their behavior around it.

That’s an important point for AI. Learning statistical regularities in the products of a culture is one thing; participating in the processes that create and revise its abstractions is another. Humans are continually negotiating what their concepts mean and whether those concepts are useful. So I would want to understand abstraction as part of a social process, with feedback and coordination, as well as a cognitive process inside an individual head.

r001.rationale: The response describes people developing abstractions together, but does not state that useful abstractions created by individuals can become part of human culture.

r002.rationale: It mentions both individual cognition and social processes, but does not clearly describe abstractions moving between individuals and culture in both directions.

r003.rationale: It contrasts learning cultural patterns with AI participating in processes that create and revise abstractions, proposing AI involvement in enabling new abstractions to emerge.
